Pilot Sample Size for the Budget Constrained Sequential Procedure

Source: R/seq_budget.R
seq_budget_pilot.Rd

Returns the number of observations to collect from every population before seq_budget is evaluated for the first time. The article gives no formula for the pilot size: it requires at least two observations per population, so that a sample variance exists, and leaves the rest to the researcher. This function checks that requirement and returns the chosen size as an integer.

Usage

seq_budget_pilot(m_0 = 5)

Arguments

m_0

The pilot sample size per population: a whole number of at least 2. Default 5.

Value

A length one integer giving the pilot sample size per population.

Details

Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal (2025, p. 431) advise against the minimum of two, because variance estimates from two observations are unstable, and against a pilot so large that it oversamples; in their simulations (p. 432) the pilot was 10 per population with a budget of 5,000. The default of 5 is this package's choice. The pilot is paid for from the same budget, so its cost, m_0 * sum(cost_per_group), must be well below the budget; a check whose data already cost more than the budget says so.

What the pilot size costs. A group whose pilot standard deviation happens to come out small meets its criterion at once, and it is sampled again only if the other standard deviations fall. With a very small pilot this is common: the group is left with two or three observations, and the variance of the contrast, estimated from them, comes out far too small. The table gives the coverage of the 95 percent interval and, in parentheses, the rejection rate of the noninferiority test at nominal level 0.05 with the true contrast exactly at the margin, from 10,000 simulated studies per cell (standard error about 0.002). The first design has the standard deviations, weights, and unit costs of the normal row of the article's Table 1 (costs 38, 15, and 10; a budget of 5,000, which buys about 40 to 100 observations per group); the second has those of the example on the seq_budget_sensitivity page (the same costs; a budget of 1,500, about 15 to 28 per group). Each was run with normal and with right skewed populations.

BudgetPopulationsPilot of 10Pilot of 5Pilot of 2
5,000normal0.947 (0.055)0.949 (0.053)0.928 (0.063)
5,000skewed0.937 (0.040)0.939 (0.043)0.903 (0.060)
1,500normal0.938 (0.060)0.931 (0.060)0.896 (0.081)
1,500skewed0.924 (0.054)0.907 (0.075)0.852 (0.121)

With a pilot of 2 the estimated variance of the contrast averaged only 0.59 to 0.76 of the true variance of the estimator, and the true variance was 1.30 to 1.51 times the smallest the budget allows; with pilots of 5 and 10 the two figures were 0.86 to 0.99 and 1.01 to 1.06. In the pilot of 2 runs with normal populations, 6 percent (budget 5,000) and 18 percent (budget 1,500) of the studies ended with a group of two or three observations, and the interval covered the contrast in 0.64 and 0.73 of those studies against 0.94 of the rest. A pilot of 5 or 10 costs little when the budget buys 40 or more observations per group. When it buys fewer than about 30, or the populations may be skewed, 10 is the safer choice, and a pilot of 2 should not be used. seq_budget_sensitivity gives the figures for a design of interest through its m_0 argument.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., Bandyopadhyay, T., Kelley, K., & Padalunkal, J. J. (2025). A sequential approach for noninferiority or equivalence of a linear contrast under cost constraints. Psychological Methods, 30(2), 425–439. doi:10.1037/met0000570
